tip: Movement toward a place puts 'in' with the accusative: 'in den Supermarkt' answers 'wohin' (where to).
German makes being glad reflexive: 'ich freue mich' literally I gladden myself, while English just says I'm happy.
After 'einen', a masculine accusative adjective ends in '-en': 'einen starken Kaffee'.
'Sich Sorgen machen' puts the worrier in the dative: 'mach dir keine Sorgen' (make yourself no worries).
When something other than the subject opens, the verb stays second: 'Heute ist es kälter' puts 'ist' before the subject 'es'.
'Sich verabschieden' takes 'von' plus dative for whom you leave: 'verabschieden uns von unseren Gastgebern'.
After the definite article 'die', the adjective takes the weak ending '-e': 'die junge Frau'.
'Schenken' marks its receiver with the dative and no preposition: 'ich schenke dir ein kleines Buch'.
With no article present, the adjective itself shows the case: 'frischen Fisch' is masculine accusative.
'Noch nie' means never up to now, the negative of 'schon einmal' (ever): 'sie hat noch nie eine Kreuzfahrt gemacht'.
'Sich bedanken' uses 'bei' plus dative for the person thanked: 'bedankt sich bei allen Helfern'.
Lowercase 'morgens' with '-s' means in the mornings as a habit; 'der Morgen' is one specific morning.
A fixed position with no movement puts 'über' in the dative: 'hängt über dem großen Esstisch' answers 'wo' (where).
'Glauben' takes the dative for a person: 'ich glaube ihm' (I believe him), never 'ihn'.
'Nicht einmal' means not even, stronger than plain 'nicht': 'er hat nicht einmal versucht'.
'Sich erinnern' uses 'an' plus accusative for what you recall: 'an nichts Besonderes ... erinnern'.
'Kein einziges' stresses not a single one, more emphatic than 'kein': 'sie besitzt kein einziges Paar'.
'Sich anmelden' is separable: the prefix 'an' jumps to the clause end, 'er meldet sich nie ... an'.
'Während' (during) normally takes the genitive: 'während der Besprechung', not 'während die Besprechung'.
'Wachsen' forms its perfect with 'sein' – it describes a change of state: 'ist gewachsen'.
'Gefallen' takes the dative: 'das Konzert hat mir nicht gefallen' means it did not please me, so I didn't like it.
The contraction 'zur' is 'zu' + 'der', and 'zu' always takes the dative: 'zur Beförderung'.
With no article in front, the adjective itself carries the case ending: 'frische Luft'.
After 'den', an adjective takes the weak ending '-en': 'den schönen Abend'.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun the adjective ends in '-es', marking the gender: 'ein scharfes Messer'.
The perfect tense usually pairs a form of 'haben' with a past participle at the very end: 'hat ein neues Auto gekauft'.
'Zu Hause' means at home (location); use 'nach Hause' for heading home.
German normally skips a verb for 'to like doing' and adds 'gern' to the action verb: 'isst gern' = likes to eat.
'Stehen' describes a fixed location, so here 'auf' takes the dative: 'auf dem Tisch', no movement.
After 'der', an adjective takes the weak ending '-e': 'der nette Herr'.
